Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
proceeded with, I wish to ask the Prime Minister a question. In a notable speech made a day or two ago by the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, the following appears, according to a despatch in the Ottawa ' Citizen ' :
The colonial secretary proceeded strongly to urge the necessity in order to preserve the great empire that the trade of the colonies should be secured. Canada had offered exceptional advantages, he said, which Great Britain did not dare accept because of the narrow interpretation of the doctrine of free trade, the policy of dictation, and interference by foreign powers, Mr. Chamberlain said he was Justified by the belief that Great Britain was so wedded to its fiscal system that it could not defend its colonies. This was a position not intended by the pioneers of free trade who, if they were alive to-day would agree to a treaty of preference and reciprocity with the empire's children. The speaker said he believed that an entirely wrong interpretation had been placed upon the doctrine of free trade but that the_country ought not to be bound by this and it should not hesitate to resort to retaliation if necessary wherever the interests between colonies and the home country were threatened.
The Right Hon. Mr. Chamberlain refers to two things : first, that Canada had made very exceptional offers to England in regard to a mutual preferential trade ; the other is that England desires to defend her colonies in case of their being attacked commercially by foreign countries. I wish to ask the government if they are prepared to lay a memorandum of these offers on the Table of the House or to take the Canadian parliament into their confidence, and give us information as to what these offers were? That I think we are entitled to. I also wish to ask whether any correspondence is being carried on with the imperial government with regard to the threatened action of Germany ; and, if so, are the government prepared to give this House any information regarding it ?

In answer to the first portion of my hon. friend's question, I may say that we have already taken the House into our confidence on the subject, for the offer which was made to the British government of a further preference as between British and foreign manufactures, is published in the Conference Blue-book as an imperial paper, to which access is easily had, and the memo, was fully read by myself in the budget speech. My hon. friend will find in that speech the offer we made the imperial authorities at the colonial conference.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: That is the only offer.
Yes. With regard to the second part of my hon. friend's question, we have had no recent correspondence with the imperial government on the action of Germany.

I would ask whether the attention of the government has been called to the alleged intention of the German government to unload upon this country a supply of ex-convicts ? The action recently taken by the United States with regard to the deportation of criminals followed by this report that the German government intends sending this class of immigrants to Canada, impels me to ask whether the government are giving the subject any attention.

We have received no official information that the German authorities contemplate any such policy. If we found that the German authorities were attempting such a policy, we would take immediate action to repeal it. My impression is that we have sufficient power, under existing laws, to deal with such a question, but if our powers should not be adequate, we shall have no hesitation in asking parliament to supplement them.

House in committee on Bill (No. S3) to incorporate the New Canadian Company, Limited.-Sir. Lemieux.
On section 1,

What is the necessity of declaring that this work is for the general advantage of Canada ?
MfV LEMIEUX. The company intend establishing a steamship company whose steamers will ply between England and Gaspe.
Although this is said to be a foreign company, I do not see the necessity of our declaring that this work is for the general advantage of Canada.

I have consulted the officers of the Department of Justice on that point. The Bill had already passed the House and was referred back, at the request of the hon. Minister of Justice, in order that some informalities might be remedied. The officers of the department gave No. 53 Vic., Chap. 104, and 84 Vic., Chap. 186, as precedents for this very clause, in the case of other English companies doing business in this country.

The declaration may be necessary to bring under the jurisdiction of the Dominion a work which would (otherwise ibe purely local or provincial. But 1 do not think that it is at all necessary that we should assume all the jurisdictions and powers of a local government even to grant a charter to a corporation to do this particular kind of work.

There were txvo considerations that entered into the matter in connection with this declaration when the Bill was before the Railway Commission. In the first place, the company is given power to carry on an ocean steamship business to foreign ports, and it was thought that possibly a question might be raised as to the power of this parliament lo pass such legislation. Therefore this clause was inserted. There is also a clause providing for the construction of tramways and other works, which come within the general definition of railways in the Railway Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: Are these supplementary to the powers the company has ns a corporation in Great Britain ? If I understand rightly, this Bill gives them all the powers they have as a corporated company in Great Britain, plus the large powers.
I do not think it gives them all the powers they have obtained under the English Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
As the clause read at first, they had all these powers, but these were restricted by the amendment.
On section 4,

The company seems to have two different entities-one in Great Britain, under which it has powers to issue bonds and debentures, and we are now giving it another set of powers in this Act. Under which entity is it to have existence here ? In this Bill we do not do away with the power of the English corporation and give it entirely a new set.

If the hon. gentleman will read the second clause as it originally was, he will see that they would have special powers and also all the powers they had under their charter in England. But, under these amendments their powers are restricted and they have only the special powers which are enumerated in the Bill. And. of course, they cannot go beyond what they have in this charter.

Under this Bill the company is ' declared a body politic and corporate within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada ; and that this Act and the Company's Clauses Act shall apply to the company and its undertaking instead of said Company's Acts of Great Britain.' It is an entirely different entity in Great Britain. The law of Great Britain applies to it over there as to the issuing of bonds, debentures. &c. The company in Canada has its powers and the company in Great Britain has its powers. That is what I say.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House in committee oil Bill (No. 121) to incorporate the Consolidated Trust Corporation.-Mr. McColl.
On section 12,

There is something strange about this clause. It enacts that the :
Honeys, properties and securities received or held by the corporations upon trust or as agent shall not be liable for the debts or obligations of the corporation.
Still,- it would seem that one of the debts or obligations of the corporation is receiving money on trust. The clause worded in this way seems to be anomalous. We ought to add, at any rate, that the moneys received on trust by the corporation shall be liable for the payment of the trust.

The purpose is, whether it is clearly expressed or not, that these trust funds shall be liable to the trustees and not for the general purposes of the corporation. If they have not expressed that, I have no doubt that is what they intended.
On section 18,

Does the minister think that this is a very wise provision ? We provide in section 18 :
The powers and authority hereby granted to the corporation shall not have any force or effect in any province in any respect in which they are inconsistent with the laws of such province.
1 am afraid there are a great many provisions in this Bill which are at variance with the ordinary law respecting trusts in our own province, but still, when we have a trustee I do not think we should put that limitation upon the company's powers.

I think it will probably be understood to mean that inasmuch as the management of trusts is a matter coming under the authority of the provincial law this Act can affect only them in so far as the provincial law will permit it. We cannot regulate ordinary trustees. This happens to belong to the class of subjects in which there is both provincial and Dominion authority-provincial authority as to the regulation of the trust, and Dominion authority as to the regulation of the company. A trustee is only permitted under provincial authority to invest his money in certain directions, and this Bill could not change that authority'. I think that is what they are particularly aiming at.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
House in committee on Bill (No. 128) for the relief of William Francis Schooley.- Mr. Boyd.
On the preamble,

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise for the purpose of opposing the reporting of this Bill. I notice that according to the allegations of the Bill the former wife of Mr. Schooley abandoned him fourteen years ago, that she obtained a decree of divorce in one of the American states eleven years ago and that she married in the state of Michigan five years ago. These statements, assuming them to be facts, and as such they appear upon the record, would entitle Mr. Schooley to a divorce beyond question, but I rise to point out the imperfection of our law in regard to the granting of decrees of divorce. Mr. Schooley lives in Manitoba. The business of prosecuting this suit in Ottawa is one that would involve very serious expense. If Mr. Schooley was entitled to relief under our laws he has been subjected to a hardship, and to a cost in this matter that would seem to be unjustifiable, and I rise to point out that in cases where the law provides a remedy, in cases where the circumstances warrant the granting of divorce some more speedy and less expensive method should be adopted. If Mr. Schooley had been permitted to appeal in this case to a judge in Manitoba near at hand, if this case had been tried before a divorce judge, and a court could be established without additional cost by merely putting that additional duty upon the judges there, he could have obtained his relief speedily and he could have obtained it at small cost. He lias been debarred for five years from making this attempt which he is now making to get justice to which he is entitled. In all of these proceedings we are pursuing a course which is entirely unjustifiable, a course which is expensive and one which in many cases, I have no doubt, prevents people who are entitled to relief from obtaining that relief because of the difficulties attending this course of procedure, because of the expense of coming from a distant province to the capital of the country and of the attendant expense and worry of prosecuting this appeal.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

That a message be sent to the Senate to return to that House the evidence, &c., taken before the Standing Committee of the Senate,- to whom was referred the Bill No. 12S (letter B of the Senate), intituled : 'An Act for the relief of William Francis Schooley.'

Mr. Speaker, I think, before that motion is put, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) having made some reference to the subject of divorce, it does seem to me that the law as it now stands is a rich man's law as against the poor man. I think where the case is such as the hon. gentleman has described, and as the evidence bears out a more rea-

sonable method ought to be adopted whereby a man might be placed in a position to secure a divorce at less cost than the applicant now before the House has been subjected to. I think the government ought lo be in a position to make some kind of statement in reply to the speech of the hon. member for North Norfolk. This is a very important question. I, for one, do not wish to encourage the granting of divorces, but at the same time a circumstance of this kind is one that should be considered and no undue hardship should be placed upon a man who has been so unfortunate as this man has been.

Mr. Speaker, I think this is a case that ought to appeal to the sense of the House. The very fact of a man having to come down to the Senate here all the way from Manitoba is evidence to the House that there should be some better way of dealing with divorces than exists in the Dominion at the present time. This case would be settled in about half a day by a judge of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia. I think that public opinion will in time compel the government to do something so that people will not be put to this expense. If this were a poor man he would have been obliged to exist without any redress all his lifetime,' but because he is in good circumstances he is enabled to come down and seek redress through this-I was going to say-inhuman channel of obtaining it. In all cases if any British subject is aggrieved there should be some way of obtaining redress and that as quickly as possible.

This covers a rather extensive area.

I can see no good reason why the area should not be as extensive as described here for the purposes of irrigation and canals and other useful works. If the work is useful, it will be useful throughout a large area.
That is right. I do not think we should stop the Bill on account of the extent of the area unless it gives exclusive rights, which I do not think this does.

I do not wish to insist upon the point I have raised, asking for information, but it strikes me really that this is a very indefinite definition of the territory covered by this Bill, and of the powers of the company. It clearly covers one degree of latitude a distance of seventy miles, and all west of the one hundred and tenth degree of west longitude. This is an enormous area. They can operate through to the Pacific ocean if they desire to go so far. When we are granting powers of this indefinite and general character, we ought to have information as to the object of the company. I do not wrish to obstruct the passage of the Bill, but I do not suppose it would interfere with its progress to have it lie over until we have more definite information.

What does the minister say is meant by the expression here ' and other purposes ' ? It seems to go further than is necessary for an irrigation company.

This might turn out to be a waterworks company.
The promoters of the Bill claimed that the object was to use the water for milling and other purposes.

There cannot be an objection to allowing the water to be used for any purpose. If you are giving them the powers to make the canals and take the water, why not use it for fire purposes, for milling purposes or any other ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This matter was brought in question in the committee that considered this Bill. The river, in this case, I understand is Milk river. It flows through a section which this company intends to irrigate. But they might utilize the water so as to prevent it flowing on for the benefit of a part of the country which is now irrigated naturally by the river. This is arid so far as the production of cereals is concerned, but I understand that it is good grazing country. I think it is a very serious question whether we should allow one company to control all the water in the river, and, perhaps, so lessen the flow of the river as to deprive the settlers who have taken up the land for ranching purposes, of water for their cattlo.
No doubt, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) would be right in his conclusions if his premises were sound.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would ask the hon. minister to tell me in what way they are not sound ?

I was just going to call attention to that point. In the first place, this Bill does not confer any exclusive right. It is open to parliament to incorporate as many irrigation companies as it pleases for that territory. We have not deprived ourselves of the jurisdiction merely because we give this company the right to construct these canals and irrigate a portion of the territory. Moreover, we do not give to this company the power to divert the waters of the rivers. The only way in which they can take property which they do not buy by private contract, is by availing themselves of the expropriation powers contained in the General Railway Act, and I cannot conceive of their expropriating a river. I know they would not get permission to divert a river or deflect it. That is not a supposable case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
We are not supposing anything. But the understanding in the committee was that they had power under the Bill to take the water out of the river for the purposes of the company. If not, what use is the Bill ?
Mr. McCarthy.
They have not the power to divert or deflect the river.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not say they had. But they might so diminish the quantity in the river that it might be useless for a part of the section of the country through which it flows.
Under section 7, of the Act, it provides that ' The company may draw from rivers and other waters, the waters necessary for the purposes of the company.' That is rather unlimited power.
I have not read the whole Bill, and I think it did not come before the Railway Committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No, it came before the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills.

The Railway Committee had a Bill of this kind before it a year or two ago, and I think we went into it pretty carefully, and provided what we thought were the necessary safeguards. I cannot answer for this Bill, for I had not seen the Bill until this moment. I can see that some of the clauses, as for instance, clause 0, would need to be materially altered. But I do not see any objection to the conferring of powers given under section 4.
On section 5,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This section has been amended so as to read as follows :
The company may acquire and dispose of lands in the district within which the company is authorized to operate, provided that the total quantity of land to he held by the company at any one time shall not exceed two thousand square miles.
Is it a land company as well ?

Not referring to the quantity of land-I do not know whether two thousand square miles would be deemed an excessive quantity or not-it is to be noted that this company asks to be incorporated for irrigation purposes and not to be created with the powers of a land company. But under this clause they would be authorized to deal in lands. Certainly, the section is defective in that way. It ought to be provided that the company may acquire the lands necessary for the purposes for which the company is authorized, and may dispose of lands which it does not require for those purposes. We always give such power.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I would say to the minister that it goes a good deal further

than that, as I understand it. The promoters say that there are lands higher than the waters to be taken by the company would enable them to irrigate. They want to get control of all the lands ; then, they could irrigate a certain portion of every lot-say fifteen, twenty or thirty acres for each two hundred acre lot-thus providing an area in which cereals and vegetables could be grown, but enabling them to sell the whole lot.

I would say to my hon. friend that I think I understand the object of the Bill. It is for the purpose of irrigating a section of land which was granted to a railway company from Lethbridge to the boundary, of which Mr. Gault was the proprietor. A portion of that land was sold to the Mormon settlement near Milk river. They have irrigation works there which are a credit to the North-west Territories and a benefit to the people, and the land there is flourishing now in consequence. This company was formed to take over the rest of the land for the purpose of irrigating it and selling it to the actual settlers. The object of the company seems to be a bona fide one, and a worthy one. namely, the development of that section of the country. I cannot understand what objection there can be to the Bill. It is clear from what I understand, that the object of the Bill is to authorize the taking over of these lands which were granted to this coal company of which Mr. Gault was the president. an English company, for the purpose of irrigating that portion of the land and selling it to actual settlers. The land as it is now is entirely worthless, but when irrigated it will become valuable, and will be sold to settlers. As my hon. friend says, the promoter of the Bill ought to be here to explain it to us. We know nothing about it, and we have a right to explanations.

Mr. CLARKE-by Mr. Lancaster-asked
1.	Has the attention of the government been called to the verdict, or is the government aware of the fact, that the coroner's jury empanelled to inquire into the cause of the railway accident which occurred at West Lome, Ontario, on the 29th day of April, 1903, as a result of which three trainmen were killed, have returned the following verdict :-' That Thomas Luton, John McNeil, and John Elgar, on the 29th day of April, at the unincorporated village of West Lome, came to their deaths as a result of a rear end collision between two trains on the Lake Erie and Detroit River Railway. And we find that the said collision was caused by the culpable neglect of the Lake Erie and Detroit River Railway Company, in not adopting a proper system as to the running of their trains, and of not furnishing and supplying to their trainmen proper rules, so intelligible to their employees that no misunderstanding could arise as to the duties of their trainmen. We further recommend that semaphores he forthwith constructed on the said railway, at proper distances from the station.
2.	In view of the foregoing verdict, is it the intention of the government to forthwith institute a full and exhaustive inquiry, on oath, into the causes which culminated in the accident

above referred to ? And if it shall appear, after such inquiry, that the verdict of the said coroner's jury was justified by the facts, is it the intention of the government to proceed against, or to cause to be proceeded against, the responsible officials of the said company, who are declared to have been guilty of culpable neglect, as a result of which the three trainmen above named were killed ?
3.	_Has the government yet been able to find an Individual possessing the precise qualifications that would enable him to act for and on behalf of the government, in conducting full and exhaustive inquiries and investigations into the causes of railway accidents which may occur in Canada from time to time ?
4.	If no such individual has yet been found, what steps, if any, are the government taking to secure the services of such an individual ?
5.	Were the rules under which the trains of the Lake Erie and Detroit River Railway Company are operated in Canada, submitted to and approved by the government ; and if so, on what date were such rules authorized by the government ?

The attention of the government has not been called to the verdict of the jury in the case mentioned, but if the facts are as stated in the question, it would appear to devolve upon the provincial authorities, as charged with the administration of criminal justice, to take any action which might be proper in the premises.
The government has not yet been able to select a person possessing the precise qualifications for taking charge of investigations in case of railway accidents, but are on the alert to secure just such a person as is required.
In the meantime a temporary appointment has been made, and an investigation held in the case of the Windsor Junction collision on the Intercolonial Railway.
I am informed that no rules were submitted by the Lake Erie and Detroit River Railway Company for the approval of the government.

Civil service employees in the Post Office Department are insured by the department direct under the assessment principle. House again in committee on Bill (No. 39) to make further provision for the prevention of cruelty to animals, and to amend the Criminal Code, 1892.-Mr. Brock.

I did not happen to he present when this Bill was called the other day, and I understand that the matter was referred to by the Minister of Justice, who, I presume, would be looking at the questions involved purely from a legal standpoint. It appears to me that some of the provisions of the Bill would have a prejudicial bearing in respect to railway traffic. I shall call his attention to one or two considerations which perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) would think it worth considering before proceeding with the Bill further. The hon. gentleman desires that the word ' animal ' should have a wider interpretation than it now has an the Criminal Code, and that it shall not only include cattle and other animals, but domestic animals, such as cats and dogs. It would not be practicable to do that. The general law does not contemplate the extension of the meaning of the word animal to such an extent as to embrace cats, dogs and other domestic animals. It would make these provisions of the present Criminal 102J
Code comparatively unworkable, and would not fit the case, under the general scope of the Bill after it had been amended as the hon. gentleman proposes. Its bearing on the railways is, first, in this direction. Certain provisions are to be found in the sections which the hon. gentleman proposes by a sub-clause to amend, which appear to go as far in the way of requiring cattle to be looked after while in transit as parliament at the time thought it was expedient to go, so as to ensure their being made as comfortable as possible, watered and fed, and when unladen, provided with fresh hay and straw for bedding. In actual experience it has transpired that there is really more hazard in requiring that the cars should be provided with bedding of this description, by reason of the danger of fire, than there is of advantage to the railways which at present have discretion in the matter, and which do not provide bedding of that character. It is said that hay and straw, for a while after it is put in, until it has become saturated or moistened, is very likely to take fire ; and occasions of this kind have occurred. We have therefore to reflect whether or not we would do well to impose on the railway companies the obligation proposed by these clauses of my hon. friend's Bill, when it would be attended with these possible difficulties and dangers. Then, my hon. friend would have the law so changed as to require certain constructions to be provided in the car whereby animals would be kept separate in a particular way. What actually happens now on most of the railways, is this. The railway companies put up loose boards in such a way as to keep the animals apart at the start, but after the train is on its way these are removed because they say they do more harm than good. But my hon. friend would have these partitions put up as fixtures. That would entail a good deal of work and injure the cars,- and could be only of use a very short time. The objection to section one, is that it makes the expression ' animal ' include all animals, which is contrary to the general tenor of the Criminal Code. 'The objection to section two is that it would apply to dogs and cats as well as to sheep and hogs. Another objection is that, no matter how short the distance these animals have to be carried, whenever a stoppage takes place, fresh bedding must be put in. Perhaps it it might only be a few hours before the cars would be unladen again. For instance, when cattle are carried from Montreal to Halifax, after they reach Moncton, they are driven out watered and fed, and it is only a very few hours when they get to Halifax. To impose on the shipper the expense of furnishing fresh bedding in such a case would be subjecting him to an unnecessary additional charge. I quite see the object my hon. friend lias in view, and it is one which, appeals to our humanity, but we should consider the circumstances. On most of our routes the cattle are not kept

very long in the car. Under no circumstances are they kept over thirty hours without being let out and watered and fed and given an opportunity to move around. Even if they had to lie down on the bare floor, that would not hurt them, and the railway companies have found from actual experience that to put in fresh bedding increases the liability to fire, which it is very important to avoid. I do not know what suggestion to offer my hon. friend as I have not reached any conclusion, but he may be able to make some suggestions.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
Straw need not necessarily be employed, but some other less inflammable material, such as tan-bark or sawdust or sand. The main object of this Bill is to have the animals kept separate, so that the smaller animals may not be ill-treated by the larger ones. This Bill would not apply to nineteen-twentieths of our cars as not more than that proportion are used for carrying animals of various or assorted classes. The other day my attention was drawn in Toronto to the fact that some cattle shipped from Owen Sound had trampled under foot a number of small animals, such as sheep and in some cases hogs. A kind of stampede took place, the cattle rushed about, and the big animals crushed the smaller ones to death. It would be a very trifling matter for a railway company to put up some scantling divisions, strong enough to prevent the cattle from breaking through. If that were done, it would meet the object of this Bill. I am not speaking of cattle shipped over a short distance, say from Montreal to Moncton, but of those shipped a long way west of Winnipeg and which come through to the sea coast. In such cases, whenever a car is emptied, it should be cleaned out. The condition those cars get into In a day or two is something terrible, and the Bill provides that such ears should be cleaned out. The cost of supplying tan-bark, sawdust or other material not inflammable would be so infinitesimal that the companies or shippers would not object to paying it. The other day I passed a car with two dead cattle in it from the North-west. The car was not very far from Ottawa, and no doubt those animals had been trampled upon by heavier cattle, and the flooring of the cars was so slippery with slush that it was difficult for the cattle to keep their feet. The hon minister objects to railway companies being obliged to put up these heavy partitions in a great many cars, but they will be required in only a very few cai's from a very few points. People do not ship lambs and smaller cattle in large quantities from great distances. There is very seldom a whole car load of lambs. They are usually put in with other cattle and they should be partitioned off from the larger animals. The objection raised about cats, dogs, &e., does not apply to this Bill. We do not ask that cats and dogs Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
and canaries should be partitioned off from other animals, but when driven to town in a farmers wagon, they should be under some kind of supervision and not subjected to the extreme cruelty of being packed closely in a crate so that they can scarcely move. I have seen a package of game sent in such a state that no one who saw them would want them on his table. I am promoting this Bill at the instance of the Toronto Humane Society, which gets no public grants and no civic grants, and is supported entirely by the people of Toronto and Ontario. I am glad to see that this society is spreading in the province of Quebec. This society is doing good work without any pecuniary reward, and I submit that the government should endeavour to meet its views as much as possible. But, if they cannot let the Bill pass exactly as it is, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways might get such a Bill framed as they think in fairness they could ask the railways to submit to, and that would be acceptable to the House and the country. We are not demanding every particular in the Bill, but we should like a Bill framed by the Minister of Justice to meet the case as far as possible and to go as far as would be acceptable to the Minister of Railways.

It seems that part of this Bill is already provided for under the Criminal Code, in subsection 5 of section 514, which provides :
Where cattle are unladen from cars for the purpose of receiving food, water and rest, the railway company then having charge of the cars in which they have been transported shall, except during a period of frost, clear the floors of such cars, and litter the same properly with clean sawdust or sand before reloading them with live stock.
Thus, there is no provision in the Criminal Code for littering the floors of cars at first, but it is provided that this must be done when the cattle are taken out, before they are again put upon the car.

I think there may be some difficulty in framing this Bill, but, at the same time, it is probably required, and, with the assistance of the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways, I think we can put it in shape so as to be an improvement on the present law. With reference to the question of danger from fire, also the question of cost and matters of that kind, I think we should be able to get over the difficulties. It appears to me that there would be no great danger from fire in cattle cars, except that fire might be communicated from some external cause for these cars are not likely to be very inflammable. But. at all events, and as the Minister of Railways has said, the difficulty exists only for a short time, and would only exist with regard to certain materials, such as hay and straw. It is a very easy matter, if the railway companies find there is actual

danger of fire from this cause, to dampen the hay or straw before it is put in the cars, so as to overcome the danger. We cannot in any way improve the law without giving some apparent ground for an argument on the other side. But we must look to the preponderance of benefit, and it seems clear to me that the advantage would be in the enactment of such a law as this. As to the cost, I understand the minister to say that it would be unfair to the railways if this were required with regard to short distances. The necessity for littering or bedding the cars hardly exists in the case of short distances, and if you take this Bill in the spirit in which the promoter brings it before the committee, feeling at liberty to make alterations where it may be necessary, we can surely modify the Bill so as to provide that this shall! apply only where animals are to be carried for a long distance. As to the separation of animals, I think the promoter of the Bill has said all that need to be said, and I think he lias shown that this is a very necessary amendment for the safe carriage of animals. I do not think the lion. Minister of Railways followed carefully the wording of the subsection 5A of section 2 of the Bill. It provides that:
No smaller animal shall be confined or carried In the same car, van or vessel with any larger animals of different species, unless a suitable and substantial partition

-and so on. It does not apply to the difference in size of the animals ns such, but to a difference of size and species.

In the city of Montreal we see a great deal of the abuses which this Bill of my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) is intended to remove. We have a very large number of cattle arriving there, and I have myself seen instances of cruelty. I understand the difficulty which the Minister of Railways has referred to. But I would point out to the minister that the only change which this Bill makes in the law is that contained in subsection 5A, for, as my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) lias shown, the amendment to subsection 5 of section 514 is substantially what is contained in the existing law.
It is not compulsory now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think it is.

Only where the cars are stopped to unload the cattle. The subsection provides :
Where cattle are unladen from cars for the purpose of receiving food, water and rest, the railway company then having charge of the cars in which they have been transported shall, except during a period of frost, clear the floors of such cars, and litter the same properly with clean sawdust or sand before reloading them with live stock.
There is nothing to say that the cars shall be littered prior to the time of their being
unloaded for the purpose of feeding, watering or resting the cattle.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think, that in that respect the change is, perhaps, a wise one. The necessity for the change here proposed of prohibiting the crowding of small animals with large animals of a different species is one of which I have seen examples. If it were possible to embody this provision in the law, I think it would be a very great advantage.

The trouble is that the cattlemen send mixed cars of cattle and hogs, or sometimes cattle and sheep, because it reduces the cost of transportation, a larger number being put in the car. I thought there was a provision in the law prohibiting this, but I do not see it. I think this is a provision which should be made. When the cars are crowded in this way it results in the death of many animals, and, even where the animals are not killed they are left in such a condition that, when they are slaughtered, their flesh is not in as good condition for eating as if the animals had been kept separate.

There are some sections of this Bill which concern exclusively the transportation companies, and ought to be dealt with by an amendment to the Railway Act. My difficulty commences with the first section, which purports to amend section 3 of the Criminal Code. The difficulty there is very serious, because we are asked to amend section 3 of the Criminal Code by adding thereto the paragraph (ff). We are met with this anomaly, that in subsection d of section 3 of the Code, the word * cattle ' is to be found, and is defined, and it includes a large number of animals that it is intended to describe by subsection (ff). So you would have two different descriptions of the same word in the same section of the Criminal Code. This form of amendment is quite inartistic, to say the least of it. Now we have to deal with the expression * animal.'
The expression animal includes any horse, mare, gelding, bull, ox, cow, heifer, steer, calf, mule, ass, sheep, lamb, goat, pig, hog, sow, dog! cat, and every other domestic animal, fowl, or bird, or wild animal, cow, or bird captured, tamed or domesticated.
Just fancy incorporating that clause in the Criminal Code and making the word ' cattle,' where it is found in the Code applicable to such a clause as that. Why, you might even fine a man if he carries a canary bird in a cage that is not properly littered. Section 514 of the Code is to be amended. The whole of that section has reference to cattle, so you see the real word defined is ' animal.' So you have to reconstruct the whole articles of the Criminal Code which have reference to this. One does at first sight see how the economy of the statute may be entirely upset by such a

definition as this. So with reference to section 3, for instance. My hon. friend provides that the right of entry provided for in section 515 of the Criminal Code may he exercised in or upon any car, van, truck, vehicle or cockpit. That would, by implication, legalize the keeping of a cockpit. 1 do not know if there are any gentlemen in this House interested in these things, hut if there are, they would he interested to know that, though section 513 makes it illegal to keep a cockpit, here the effect of this section would be to legalize entry into a cockpit. I think there are inconveniences, to say the least of it, in this Bill if it is alloived to go through.
I suggested the other day to my hon. friend that perhaps this Bill might be considered by the draughtsman of the department, who is in the habit of drawing amendments and suggesting amendments to the Criminal Code. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) has not met Mr. Fraser, who I asked to call on him, and he did call, but in all probability they did not come together on account of the absence of my hon. friend. I would suggest that with respect to the first and third clauses, he should allow me to send Mr. Fraser to him for the purpose of seeing whether they cannot agree upon some amendment that would carry out the laudable objects that he has in view. With respect to the second section, I am afraid I must leave him to the tender mercies of the Minister of Railways and Canals.

I would point out with respect to section 2 that bedding of hay and straw is used in certain box cars in which stock is shipped on the railways now. But this would apply to what is known- as slat-cars. At the end of the journey there would probably be no stock in the car at all by reason of being set on fire from the sparks of the engine.

I understand that my hon. friend in charge of the Bill is not wedded to this particular form, and I quite agree with the Minister of Justice that it would be almost impossible to pass the Bill in its present shape on account of difficulties in the present form of the Criminal Code. But I see no reason why it could not be changed, if it is considered advisable to make some changes. Especially do I think there ought to be a strong attempt to compel railway companies to carry animals of different species separately. We must also keep in view the question of the cost of transportation. The competition in the carriage of animals is very keen. Therefore the producer and the transportation company are the two classes most affected by this Bill. I think it is proper to compel the company to divide their car into compartments for the different species of animals, because it is too bad to see sheep and hogs and big cattle huddled together in the same car, Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
and there ought to be some way to prevent it at the least possible cost. It has been suggested that the animals should be specified by name that are to be thus carried, but, from what the Minister of Justice says, that would be difficult to work out. Then as to the right of search as set forth in the Bill, that also is a matter that would require consideration. It seems to me that the Department of Justice is bound to see that this Bill is properly constructed, and if there are difficulties in the Bill in its present form, the Department of Justice should devise some amendments to overcome those difficulties.

It will be necessary to drop the first clause altogether because you could not give any such interpretation to the word ' animal ' as has been proposed here. As to the second clause, if it is the sense of the committee that it would be a proper thing to require that all cars carrying cattle shall be bedded in this description with straw, hay, sawdust, sand, tan bark, shavings or such other dry material. I think the better plan would be to reinsert the word ' cattle ' in place of ' animals.' The word ' cattle ' is defined in the Bill and it would be only in reference to cattle that any such provision as this would apply. If you insert the word 'cattle ' for the word ' animals ' in both parts of this section that would include all such animals as require to be bedded. But, before adopting this Bill, I think we ought to hear what the people have to say who have had the largest experience in regard to the carriage of cattle. Whether we agree with them or not I think it is wise for us to know what their views are upon the subject and see how this legislation is going to affect the cattle shipping business. It would not be desirable under any circumstances to pass even that section as it now stands. Then, I would say in regard to the next subsection that ' cattle ' has been defined in the original Act to include sheep, goats and swine. No smaller cattle, such as sheep, goats or swine, shall be confined or carried in the same car unless such and such precautions are taken -that would cover the ground the hon. gentleman desires to see covered. I could not recommend the committee to adopt a clause such as this until we hear more on the subject and perhaps the hon. gentleman would consent to the committee rising and reporting progress.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am quite well aware that the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) and the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) are very anxious to promote this Bill in such a way that it will be of some use and that it will have something good in it. There is no use in the Bill going through in such a way that it will not carry out the object of the society

I represent, and which has in view particularly to stop the practice of animals of various sizes and species being indiscriminately crowded into one car; that is driving in a drove of cattle first of all, and then driving in sheep and hogs and filling up every foot of space under these cattle. We want to put a stop to that. Another object is that where two species of animals are placed in the same car there shall be a partition between them. We had a case the other day, as some hon. gentleman are no doubt aware, where .three or four calves were placed in a car with a drove of iiogs. there being a very light partition between them. They arrived at the station but the smaller animals were dead. The calves had been eaten up by the hogs in the car. These hogs were afterwards used for human food and I want to avoid any abominable thing of that kind taking place. I do not think we should leave it to the experience of the cattle men.
I do not either, but I would like to hear what they have to say.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Decidedly, but I think we should be protected against their opinions if they are adverse to the adoption of reasonable and humane methods in carrying on this traffic. I am quite well aware that the hon. Minister of Justice and the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals are as anxious as I am that a Bill that will deal with the cases I speak of should be passed and therefore I am willing to leave it to be amended in such a way as will make it satisfactory to the country generally. I move that the Committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Campbell for the second reading of Bill (No. 20) to amend the Weights and Measures Act.

I think we would require some explanation of this Bill. It affects a great many interests in the vicinity of the city of Montreal. I am not in a position to say to what extent it affects these interests, but I think it would be desirable that we should know why this new measure is introduced.

Mr. Speaker, I explained the objects of this Bill the other day when it was before the House, but the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was not present, I think. The BUI is intended to apply more particularly to the province of Ontario. It has become the custom in the province of Ontario to sell milk by the can. In the city of Toronto
there are about 3,000 cans of milk per day sold. These are purchased from the farmers all around within twenty, thirty or forty miles of the city. Wrlien the plan which has been in vogue for a good many years was first adopted, cans were all made to hold eight gallons, but there is nothing on the statute-book to-day, I believe, to say what the can shall be, whether it shall be eight gallons, or ten gallons, or whatever it may be, but there was an unwritten law that eight gallons should constitute a can of milk. However, as time went on, the cans made by the dealers in the city have been constantly enlarged, first to eight and one-quarter gallons and eight and one-half gallons, and on until to-day there are none less than eight and one-half gallons, while a great many hold nine gallons of milk. The farmers, are obliged to fill these cans. After carrying the milk eight or ten miles it would not be good for it if the cdns were not full. They are obliged to fill the cans and as a consequence they lose half a gallon or more on every can of milk they sell. That amounts to a very large sum in the aggregate and the Bill simply provides that when a person sells a can of milk that means eight gallons and that a half a can is four gallons. By arrangement with the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) it was agreed that the second reading of this Bill should take place and that it should then be referred to a special committee. I am prepared to leave it to a special committee if the House sees fit to grant the second reading of the Bill. I am sure that this Bill is a step in the right direction. It affects nobody ; it is going to injure nobody.
What good is it then !
It prevents the farmer who sells his milk from being obliged to supply half a gallon for every can more than he gets paid for.

My hon. friend (Ml-. Campbell) states that the object of this motion is to have the Bill referred to a special com-' mittee and for my part I have no objection. I do not think that the custom which the hon. gentleman says exists in Ontario obtains in Quebec and it was in the section about the application of this new measure to the province of Quebec that I saw some difficulty, but if it is going to be referrrd to a committee I have no objection.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not in his seat, as he would be prepared to discuss this Bill. 1 may state that the government do not feel disposed to accept the Bill at the present time. It requires some consideration, and the matter is now undergoing the consideration of the Department of Justice. I will not say that the government will be prepared next session to introduce legislation on this subject; but since the matter has been brought to the attention of the House, most of the provinces have amended their laws with regard to insolvent estates, and I understand that these are now pretty satisfactory except in one or two provinces. It is to be hoped that the provinces themselves will attend to this kind of legislation, and adopt laws of such a character as to be acceptable. In regard to the hon gentleman's Bill, I understand from the Minister of Justice that the principle of it is perhaps acceptable, though the government are not prepared to accept all of its provisions. Under these circumstances, if my hon. friend persists in his motion, I must ask the House to reject it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was induced to bring this measure to the notice of the House because of the general desire which exists through the country, particularly among the commercial classes, that we should have uniform legislation on the subject of insolvency throughout the whole Dominion of Canada. I know for a fact that such is the desire of all the commercial bodies in the Dominion.
I must call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that having already spoken on the question, lie has not the right to speak again.
I thought I had the right to sum up the discussion on my motion.

No. When a member moves an order of the day, he has the right to speak only once. So, when a Bill stands for a second reading, the member who moves the Bill has a right to speak once when he makes the motion, but he has no right to reply.

Well, Mr. Speaker, with your permission, and with the indulgence of the House, I may perhaps be allowed to mention that I have received from the Secretary of the Montreal Board of Trade a letter in which he urges strongly that this Bill should receive the immediate attention

of the House. I have also received a letter from the secretary of the Chambre de Commerce, conveying the same information; and I may perhaps read to the House a resolution which was adopted on the first of April, in respect to this law. This is the resolution :
The Chamber of Commerce of the District of Montreal.
Report of the Committee on Legislation, adopted at the meeting of April 1, 1903, Insolvency Act.
The progress of Canada, the expansion of its trade and industries, its treaties with foreign nations, the influx within its borders, of immigrants and foreign capital, all the conditions of a rapidly developing country, make it necessary that some efficient means of protection be provided forthwith in behalf of those (whatever their origin), who by engrossing its trade, contribute in such a large measure to the wealth and greatness of its people.
Such a measure of protection as will give a new impetus to commerce by restoring confidence among dealers, shielding worthy though unsuccessful merchants and setting right business transactions, can be secured only be means of an Act applicable to the whole country and making uniform the system of distribution of the assets of the parties who failed.
While this Chamber recognizes that special needs, worthy no doubt of consideration, may have heretofore prevented the various governments anxious to enact some such law, from taking any such action, nevertheless, reasons of a superior order make it more imperative than ever that trade should not be subjected to unnecessary risks, and that the good name of the country should be kept above suspicion.
Therefore, confiding in the wisdom of our rulers and of the members of parliament, this Chamber, having on all occasions urged the adoption of a new Insolvency Act, and having last year given its approval to the Fortin Bill, hopes that, all difficulties having now been removed. the said Bill will be allowed to become law in the course of this session, after due consideration has been given to certain suggestions submitted by this Chamber and various public bodies.
The whole respectfully submitted.
(Sgd.) H. A. A. BRAULT, Chairman, Committee on Legislation. (True Copy.)
The Secretary,
(Sgd.) JOS. HAYNES.
There is also a report of some length from the same committee concerning the passing of this Bill. Under the circumstances, I do not think I would he justified in abandoning the Bill at this stage.

I did not intend to say anything on this Bill, and would not have done so but for the fact that the right hon. the premier has Intimated his disposition not to allow it to go any further at the present time. It has been my opinion for a good many years that an insolvent law for Canada was very much needed, and that fact has been impressed on the attention of parliament from various sources times almost without number, whenever an insolvent law was proposed. Letters have been sent to members of this House urging that some kind of insolvent law be adopted. But of late years the commercial element of the country seems to have despaired of the prospect of parliament passing an insolvent law ; and for that reason perhaps more than any other, there has not been of late so much interest taken in the subject. The premier says that each province has its own law for the distribution of estates, which seems to give fair satisfaction. It may give fair satisfaction so far as the creditor is concerned ; but the unfortunate insolvent is left out of the question entirely, and no matter how honest or how unfortunate he may have been, he is debarred from ever starting business again.
I have known of many instances of intelligent and well-meaning business men who failed in business through influences and circumstances over which they had little or no control. They were valuable citizens and would have been valuable additions to the commercial class provided they could have started again, but owing to the fact that there was no insolvent law and they could get no relief to enable them to start again, they had to choose between going into service and eking out whatever kind of existence that might give, or leave the country and begin life again in a foreign land. The latter has been the usual course adopted. I know from personal knowledge of many worthy men who have thus left our country during the past ten or fifteen years, who otherwise would have remained in Canada and been to-day doing a profitable business in their own country. Surely we ought to provide some law for the relief of those people who have failed through no fault of their own. Surely the country ought to provide some means for enabling these people to provide for themselves and tbeir families without being compelled to try their fortunes in any other land. While tiie distribution of assets may be fair to-day to the creditors in Canada, it is altogether unfair to other creditors. Many of our merchants import largely from the old country, and over and over again I have rend letters, especially from the commercial element in England, complaining that we had no insolvency law and that there was therefore no protection to them when they sold goods to Canadians, because, in the event of failure, the Canadian creditors gobbled up the estate and there was practically nothing left for anybody else. This makes it difficult for merchants in the old country to do business at all in Canada. A good many years ago I was opposed to an insolvency law and spoke against it on several occasions, but the experience of time and observation has convinced me that I was wrong and that an insolvency law would be in the interests of Canada. True, many of the evils which developed under the old

law created a prejudice against an insolvency law, but surely we are equal to the task of eliminating these evils and providing a law that would not be open to the objections raised against the last one. X have not looked over the Bill now before us except in a very cursory manner, but it seems to have many valuable features not to be found in some of the Bills introduced some years ago. The government ought to take up this question themselves, but, as far as I am concerned, I am in favour of this Bill being proceeded with, and I am confident that we are equal to the task of making it such a measure, as will work in the interests of the commercial community as a whole and do justice both to Canadian and foreign creditors.

I am heartily in favour of the principle of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, but I agree with my right lion, friend the First Minister that a measure so important to the citizens in Canada in general should be referred to the Department of Justice before being submitted to the consideration of this House. In my opinion, an insolvency law is one of these things which we must provide in the very near future for the commercial classes of Canada. In the passage of such a law our national credit is, to a certain extent, involved. The only question which presents itself to my mind is this : Is the Bill broad enough in its application ? There was a Bill introduced some years ago by the late Sir John Abbott, which was broad in its application, but the application of which was not sufficiently clearly defined, and looking at clause three of the measure before us, I think that the same objection may be taken to it. If we are to have an insolvency law which is to be general in its application, clause three of this Bill should be more definite. In my opinion, farmers should be included with commercial traders. There are some other minor points in the Bill which will require very serious consideration, and therefore I think it will be well to refer it to the Department of Justice.

there not being uniform legislation, and it being well known in Britain, the country with which we wish to do the largest measure of trade, that there is no uniform law and that the outside creditor, whether of Britain or of any other country, has to become acquainted with several different systems of legislation in order to know what remedy he has, is seriously hampering, and has hampered our commerce and our business relations in the past. As I said before, having regard to the fact that we are rapidly expanding, having regard to the fact that by the energy, and industry, and hope, and ambition of the people of Canada, we are likely, whether there comes a wave of depression or not, to reach out still further in the future, and this at a rapid rate, I think it is the bounden duty of every member of parliament to bring his experience and ids wisdom to bear upon this matter; and it being especially one of the subjects relegated to this House by the British North America Act, to exercise our functions in this regard, and not relegate to the provinces, to work at random and with uncertainty, a matter upon which we should work for the whole Dominion.
It has been said that there are some prejudice by farmers against an Insolvency Act. I do not know whether that is so or not, I have not found that it is so. I have already referred to the fact, that the farming community and the industrial classes generally who launch out into large enterprises, should have the benefit of the provisions of an Insolvency Act. I have not found any prejudice among farmers against the passage of such an Act. Representing a distinctly rural constituency, I am prepared to take the responsibility as such representative, and say that I will at all events take all the onus that can be cast upon me by advocating what I believe to be in the interest, not especially of the commercial classes, not especially in the interest of the rural classes, but in the broad general interest of the Dominion. Believing that to be the effect, I am prepared to give this measure my support, and to work to bring it into the best possible form in the general interests of the whole of Canada.

I would ask the Prime Minister if the government would not take this Bill out of my hands completely and adopt it as a government measure, so that it might become law this session. I would be quite willing to give up the Bill.

Yes, but I am not prepared at this moment to accept the gift proffered by my hon. friend. It is a matter that requires some consideration. The government is not prepared to say that it would be advisable to introduce such legislation. All I can say at this moment is that the question is engaging our consideration.
