Sir. ROBERT BICKERDIKE (Montreal, St. I.awrenee) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 94) respecting incorporated companies. He said : Sir. Speaker, this Bill is intended to stop, if possible, men running to this House and the other House to get charters for the purpose of selling them. I have stated in the Bill that charters shall be void if not taken advantage of in two years. Some hon. members have thought this too short a time. I have no objection to changing the time. There are one or two amendments that have come from the Montreal board of trade, and if the House will agree to them I will suggest that they be put into the Bill. One proposes to amend clause 1, by inserting after the word * commence ' or the words ' or causes to be commenced,' that is to say while a company may not operate tinder its charter it may sell its charter to some other company and this other company may operate under it.

Would that amendment cover the case of the Dominion Telegraph Company ? I may say that I have had a communication respecting the effect of this Bill if passed in its present shape on the Dominion Telegraph Company and Montreal Telegraph Company, whose lines have been for many years operated by the Great North-western Telegraph Company.
That will not affect them if they are going on under another name or under another company.
Their lines are being operated by another company.
Quite so.
You are perfectly clear on that point ?
If they are being operated the Bill does not affect them. We might pass the second reading and submit it to the Minister of Justice.

I am somewhat embarrassed about giving my consent that this Bill should go to committee because I do not understand its provisions. If I understood the Bill I could give my reasons for objecting to it, but I really cannot understand what my hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike) means by this Bill. In answer to the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) the introducer said it would not affect the Dominion Telegraph Company. I have a letter from one of the officials connected with the Montreal Telegraph Company in which he says that the .Montreal Telegraph Company, leased, after many years' working, to the Great North-western Telegraph Company and now worked by it, would be wiped out if this Bill goes through. The Dominion Coal Company, leased to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and worked by the latter, would also be affected by this Bill. This letter is received from a gentleman in Montreal connected with the Montreal Telegraph Company, and if it be a fact, as he says, that that would be the result of his Bill, I cannot help objecting to it. I cannot understand what my hon. friend is driving at, what purpose lie has in view, what his object is in this legislation, and not knowing what the object of the Bill is, I am sorry that I cannot agree to the House going into committee upon it.

I think that this Bill will affect a great many other companies in addition to the Dominion Telegraph Company, and I think we should pause before passing such sweeping legislation as that. There are many companies in Quebec that still exist for some purpose, but which are not at present exercising their corporate powers. I think this legislation is very sweeping, the public has had no notice of it. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike) had better drop the Bill this session.

Mr. Speaker, I want to point out, too, that it will be utterly impossible to adopt clause 1 which I gather from what the hon. member (Mr. Biekerdike) has said, contains the principal feature of the Bill. It says :
If any company incorporated by the parliament of Canada, or under an Act of that parliament, fails to commence active operations within two years after incorporation, or fails to use any of its corporate powers during two consecutive years, such unused powers, except so far as is necessary for winding up the company, shall be forfeited.
It is well known that many companies are incorporated with several powers to be exercised by them. A company might be incorporated and might comply with the terms of its incorporation if it put into operation one or more of its powers while some other power contained in the Bill might, for some good reason, not be put into operation for some time. The result would be that though certain powers were used the unused powers, the operation of which for some good reason might be deferred to a later date, would "be destroyed.
I do not see how we could possibly adopt the principle involved in section 1. It seems to me that that objection is an insuperable one.

As it is quite evident that the leaders on both sides of the House are opposed to my Bill I ask to be permitted to withdraw it.
Motion withdrawn.
House resumed consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Puttee, for the second reading of Bill (No. 95) to amend the Conciliation Act, 1900.
Mr. Speaker, when this Bill was before the House on a former occasion, I explained it pretty thoroughly, and I do not think it is necessary to go into it again at this stage.

There are same provisions of this Bill that the government can accept and there are some that they cannot. I have no objection to the Bill going into committee with the understanding that the adoption of the second reading does not commit the House to the provisions of the Bill. The second paragraph purports to authorize the appointment of a board of arbitrators without the consent of the parties. That is contrary to the principles of the Conciliation Act. However desirable such a provision may be, I hardly think that the public are educated to that standard yet. and therefore it would be in advance of public opinion. It is true that principle is incorporated in the Bill before the House respecting railways in extreme cases, but we cannot consent to that principle in re-1 Mr. MONK.
gard to ordinary industrial troubles. Sections 3 and 6 of the Bill with certain modifications might be passed so far as the government is concerned. My hon. friend (Mr. Puttee) desires to have the Bill referred to the committee so that it may be dealt with in detail, there will be no objection.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and House went into committee on the Bill.
On section 1,

The Conciliation Act provides that a board of conciliation may be appointed on the application of the employers or the employees interested. This section provides that the board may be appointed without the application of either party. That is a material difference. Under the amendment the board may be appointed without either party applying, whereas under the present law application must be made by one or other party to the dispute.
I cannot see the effect of introducing this amendment to the present Act.
Does the minister accept tills amendment ?
I have no objection to the amendment.

My hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) will find there is a great difference between the amendment and the provision in the present Act. The amendment makes it the duty of the Labour Department to appoint a conciliator without application at all. Suppose the parties are now willing to conciliate, then when this officer is appointed he will be an investigator and will ascertain all the facts and report. It is very much the same principle that was put in the Railway Disputes Bill, and it will insure that there shall be an impartial investigation into any dispute even although *tlie parties are not willing at that time to ask for conciliation or Investigation. I believe that this amendment will have a great deal to do with putting the Act into force more frequently than formerly. I am afraid that in the future the number of strikes will increase, and some strengthening provision like this In the Conciliation Act is very desirable.

Section agreed to.
On section 2,

That paragraph cannot be accepted. It proposes to appoint arbitrators without the consent of both parties. The first clause which was assented to, appoints a conciliator who would take evidence and make an award, but this second paragraph would force arbitration on unwilling parties, and I move that it be stricken out.
Clause struck out.

On section 3,

I move to amend this section by striking out the words ' arbitrator to take evidence under oath regarding the matter in dispute; also to strike out the figure ' 5 ' in the first line and substitute therefor the figure ' 7,' so as to make it amend section 7 of the Conciliation Act instead of section 5. It will amend section 7, which deals with conciliation and provides for the conciliators making their report and the publication of the report.

Would it not be better to require a statement of that kind to be published in the 'Official Gazette' ? I have no doubt that it would also be published in the 'Labour Gazette'; but everybody does not take the ' Labour Gazette,' and I think the statement should be published in the general official publication of the country.

I think the ' Labour Gazette ' would reach a good many more people than the ' Official Gazette.' Its circulation is considerable now, and it may be treated as the official gazette of the government in labour matters.
This is the first time we have made this kind of enactment.
No, it is also referred to in the Bill which I have before the House respecting labour disputes on railways.
It is also referred to in section ten of the original Act.

I scarcely see the importance of this amendment. What effect will it have ? Is it along the line of compulsory arbitration? It does not seem to me that it is. If we are going to legislate any further on these questions, I think we had better go to the bottom of the whole matter at once and deal with it in such a way that we can bring about a settlement of labour disputes. To my mind this is only trifling with the matter. It does not touch the kernel at all. It is proposed from the standpoint of some trades and labour council who simply keep this matter alive before the workingmen of the country with the pretense that they are doing something for the workingmen, while as a matter of fact accomplishing nothing. I think it is about time that we were doing something, and if labour disputes are to be brought to a termination within a reasonable time without sacrificing the interests of the working men, or the interests of the employers, I think the time has come when we should take into consideration legislation which will compel both parties to agree to any reasonable settlement that may be suggested by those who are constituted for the purpose of bringing about a settlement. That is my opinion on the whole matter. I do not think this legislation is going to amount to anything.

' If this Bill were simply dealing with a local organization, 1 would be very well inclined to agree with it; but why should this country be so much concerned about protecting the interests of an international organization, which is not under the laws of this country, which does not recognize anything we do in this parliament except in so far as it will suit its own interests ? I contend that the labour organizations of this country should be manly enough to stand on their own feet and submit to the laws of Canada, and not be dictated to by organizations on the other side of the line. If they are not dictated to by these organizations, as some gentlemen in this House have said, then why, is this word ' international ' introduced in this Bill V Why should we allow ourselves to be dictated to by antagonistic organizations on the other side of the line ? I contend that this House should throw out any legislation of an international kind that comes before it. It is only an attempt to hold up the manufacturing and other industrial interests of this country. We have had the farmers of this country antagonised, and their freight held up at the dictation of international organizations. I contend that this country will not put up with this sort of thing, and therefore I urge the government to throw out anything that purports to legislate for any country but Canada. I notice that this Bill provides :
In no case shall a conciliator or arbitrator stipulate, nor shall it be stipulated in any agreement promoted or recommended by a conciliator, or arbitrator, that any employee shall relinquish his membership in any local, national or international trades union or labour association.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not the section we are at.
This whole Act is moving in a certain direction, and it culminates by stipulating that anything we do here should have no effect.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman be kind enough to tell me what Bill he is reading ?

Bill ninety-five. If the chairman reads it over, he will find that my remarks are perfectly in order. I do not care which clause of this Bill you take, it is not one that should be considered by this House, because we are attempting to legislate beyond our powers for an international arrangement which we cannot control. If the chairman says I am out of order, and have no right to speak, I will resume my seat.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not say the hon. gentleman is not in order, but the Bill I have does not appear to be the same as the one the hon. gentleman is reading.

That is the difficulty in connection with this whole matter. There

is an attempt to make people believe that we are passing Canadian legislation whereas we are legislating in connection with a foreign organization.

The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken. Surely he must know that this Bill can only affect Canadian unions and Canadian employers. There is no intention to go outside the jurisdiction of this parliament and we could not. It would he absurd to introduce a Bill to affect any international organization not under our control. This Bill is not intended to affect trade unions but to try and arbitrate disputes that will arise between Canadian employers and workmen. Whether the attempt be successful or not, it is worth our consideration, and we should approach the matter without prejudice or bias one way or the other. I agree with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken and deplore equally with him the fact that there is not more force in the Act. I believe that if my amendment were accepted, making arbitration possible on the application of one party, that would extend the principle as far as it can go without encroaching on compulsory arbitration. Although I am not opposed to compulsory arbitration, the majority of members here are. I am afraid that disputes will not be adjusted until we have some reasonable method of dealing with them by compulsory arbitration, and the section thrown out of the Bill, although it provided for arbitration on the request of one of the parties, did not make the award binding on either. It simply left it to the force of public opinion, on an investigation being made and an award declared by a disinterested party.
Suppose you had compulsory arbitration, how could you enforce it ? Would you put these people in jail ?

I am afraid it would not be of any use our entering into a discussion on the features of compulsory arbitration at present. In New Zealand they are getting awards observed and enforced under compulsory arbitration. In the Australian commonwealth, they are doing the same thing. The only objection to it in Canada is that the people are not ready for it. But I protest against this introduction of the question of internationalism and foreign agitators and all the rest, being brought into the subject before us. The Bill and amendment are purely along the lines of conciliation, in order to do away as much as possible with disputes of a minor character that often grow into larger ones. I believe that a conciliation Act can smoothe out some of the troubles of a minor character, but so far it has not affected any of the larger evils.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would ask hon. gentlemen to confine themselves to the discussion of clause three. On clause four, Mr. BROCK.
we will come to what the hon. gentleman is now discussing.
Has the government allowed section three to go ?
Yes.

What is there to be done by section three which is not already provided for in the Conciliation Act ? Section three provides that a conciliator shall look into the facts and suggest a settlement. Is not that already in the Conciliation Act ?

I think it is, but there seems to exist a doubt in the mind of my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), and 1 have no objection to remove it. Besides this provides that the basis of settlement shall be published in the ' Labour Gazette.' That is not to be found in the Conciliation Act.
The word used in the amendment is ' arbitrator ' instead of ' conciliator.'

He is no longer a conciliator but an arbitrator.
On section 4,
4. The said Act is further amended by inserting the following section immediately after section 6 :-
6a. In no case shall a conciliator or arbitrator stipulate, nor shall it he stipulated in any agreement promoted or recommended by a conciliator or arbitrator, that any employee shall relinquish his membership in any local, national or international trades union or labour association ; nor shall an agreement subject any employee to a penalty on account of such membership.

It has been suggested that this should be made an amendment to section eight Instead of section six, to which I have no objection. I would move that * six ' be struck out and ' eight ' be substituted.
Tlie intent of this amendment is to commend this principle of conciliation to the employees. At present the employees keep away as much as possible from conciliation or arbitration because there lias been rather a mischievous principle introduced into the awards of some arbitrators or conciliators, believing that they had power to take the by-laws or constitutions of an organization into their judgment and alter them as they saw fit. As a matter of fact, the policy is laid down by almost all associations that they will not put their constitution and bylaws to arbitration, and they are perfectly right. A clause of this kind will dff a good deal to commend the principle of this Bill to the parties interested.
Have the words ' local, national or international ' any force whatever ?
No, it seems to me that the words ' any trade union,' would be sufficient.
It seems to me that the I clause would be just as strong if we left the words ' local, national or international ' out and made it read ' any trade union or local association.'
I was about to suggest the same thing. These words might just as well be left out, if there is any objection to them.

As the labour representatives in this House are beginning to see the thing very much in the way I see it, I withdraw any objection I have to anything else, if they will withdraw the word ' international.' I therefore move that the words ' or international ' be struck out.
Why not leave it ' any trades union ' ?

I am in favour of trades unions in this country, subject to the laws of this country ; but this Bill would bring in international unions that are not subject to the laws of this country. Why need the word ' international ' be used ? Why do we send to Philadelphia, New York, Boston, or any other large American city for international interviewers, and organizers to come to this country ? We should do everything to make it thoroughly understood that the Canadian parliament is able and willing to legislate for this country and will insist upon its rights to do so. I do not care what bylaws and rules the local organizations may have, they have a perfect right to have them ; but when these local laws have to be referred to agitators from the other side of the line, that is something that we should fight against. These Canadian organizations, I am in favour of, and am anxious to support in every possible way, notwithstanding what may have been said. But I do not wish to support, nor do I think this country will support, agitations and organizations, the mainspring of which is on the other side of the line. Therefore, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) is willing that the word ' international ' be struck out, I am willing to let it pass.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) asks why organizations send across the line for men. I do not know why his organizations do so, but I know as a matter of fact they do. The Toronto Manufacturers' Association sent across the line to bring in American agitators from Dayton, Ohio, and the Metal Working Manufacturers' Association did the same thing. I do not pretend to know why these organizations did these things. I know why an ordinary trade union sends across the line, but I do not see why it is necessary to discuss this at the present time. I notice that when we have railway Bills before the House, these hon. gentlemen do not ask why the capital comes from other countries, or why the promoters are men who owe no allegi-103
ance to Canada ; and when a friendly society is to be incorporated they do not ask why it is that the headquarters of that society are in another land. They know perfectly well that we are dealing with our own subjects and that, even if the societies to which they belong are affiliated with outside organizations, that does not affect this provision, for it can control the citizens of Canada only. I am perfectly willing that all the words, ' local, national or international,' should be struck out.
It is not necessary to strike out ' local ' or ' national, ' I take it that the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) has no objection to Canadians belonging to local organizations.
Certainly not.

But the hon. gentleman does not want to be misrepresented on that point. I understand that the hon. gentleman is willing that all these organizations should enjoy all the rights they have in Canada, and does not desire to deprive them of any of those rights. If the section is amended as the hon. gentleman suggests, it will meet his views and will help to remove the ground for the contention of some hon. gentlemen that labour organizations are controlled by men on the other side of the line. Personally, I understand that many organizations in Canada are affiliated with the international associations, and that the strength they thus gain' is a benefit to the organization. I have no objection to the amendment the hon. gentleman suggests, seeing that it will meet what seems to me the paltry objection that he raised.

I agree with the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) and the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) that, in so far as this phrase is concerned, it is a term that the House should guard against. But, if you strike out the words ' local, national, or international ' you make it, in effect the same as now. I think the word ' international ' should be struck out, and that would meet the object the House has in view. There is a feeling, undoubtedly, that a good many of the strikes carried on by the trades unions are due to the work of the agitators from the other side of the line. If that feeling could be removed it would strengthen the labour element with public opinion on this side of the line.

This is another clause, it seems to me, which my hon. friend (Mr. Puttee) might have left out. I do not think the arbitrator or conciliator-for it is only the conciliator we are dealing with here-ought to be told by legislation that he shuts out any class in any suggested arrangement, or prevents any employee from belonging to a trades union. I am not aware that any conciliator or any body else has made such a



suggestion. Why should we legislate in this sense ? What the conciliator is supposed to do is to suggest a basis of arrangement between the parties, and X think it unwise for my hon. friend to raise the question by this useless piece of legislation. I cannot bring myself to agree completely with my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock). There are a great many trades unions in the city of Montreal that find it useful-for what reason I cannot exactly say-to be affiliated with American organizations or organizations of other countries. X cannot say here without having examined the question more fully that they are in the wrong. With regard to international unions being an irritating cause of strikes, I am not prepared to admit that either. What strikes and labour difficulties we have had in the city of Montreal have not been suggested by agitators from the other side. That I say from my own knowledge. I am not absolutely acquainted with the by-laws of our trades unions ; but I think it is especially provided that, before having recourse to a strike, the matter must have been fully considered by the local trades union and decided by them without any outside interference whatever. After the strike has been decided upon, then, and then only, is the question of the wisdom of striking submitted to the central council wherever that may be ; the central council-international or whatever may be its character-intervenes, as I understand it, expressly for the purpose of preventing a strike. That is what I have found out, at any rate among the working men of Montreal. These men, very far from being urged to strike, find that the central council acts the part of a conciliator. And, if after all these efforts have failed and a strike takes place, then the man whom my hon. friend from Centre Toronto regards as an agitator comes in. But, as I understand it, he is rather a man having experience in labour matters, who comes independent of all parties for the purpose of smoothing over the difficulty if possible. Under these circumstances, and upon general principles, if a workman belonging to a labour union finds it useful and for the benefit of his own association to have that association linked with one with similar aims in another country, having great power and resources, I do not see why he should not have that power. I know that in Montreal these trades unions feel that they gain power, that they can work better if they are united with similar trade unions in other countries. As some hon. gentleman has remarked, we admit foreign capital, we allow foreign capital to make combinations with our own capital. I cannot, for my part, see why we should not allow labourers to coalesce, provided they do it properly, and not In violation of any law. I really think this section is useless. My hon. friend must see that it has brought up a discussion on a matter of very Mr. MONK.
grave import which is not, strictly speaking, in question here, and he has offered to withdraw the word ' international.' But, for my part, I would like to consider the matter further before saying that I disapprove of such combinations.

The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has given us a piece of refreshing coolness in the remarks he has just made to the House with regard to disinterested and philanthropic efforts of the labour agitators on the other side, whose sole and only object in coming over here is to avert strikes and settle labour disputes amicably. Perhaps the hon. gentleman believes that is the case; if he does, I certainly do not. I believe that the operations of these emissaries, in nine cases out of ten, are in the line of promoting and fomenting difficulties. I agree with the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) in his demand that this word ' international ' should be expunged from this section. I know myself of cases where agitators, labour emissaries from the United States, have come in here and have promoted strikes, have been the cause of strikes.
Where ?

At Smith's Falls, for instance. The operation of a large manufacturer there was suspended and the men went out on strike. A labour union was formed, the men were coerced into joining that union, were compelled to do so. Two-thirds of the men who joined that union did so reluctantly and against their wishes. But the terrorism, and the influences that these men know so well how to use, were brought into play there, and the result was that the men went out on strike and the business of that concern was suspended. Three-fourths of their orders fortunately were filled, and the firm said : Very well, gentlemen, if you do not wish to work, if you decide to dictate to us how we shall carry on our business, we will simply suspend operations. They did suspend operations, and after the strike had continued a month the men came back to work, and three-fourths of the men that came back, I am told, were opposed to having gone out on a strike. It seems to me we are largely engaged here in performing the operation of a tail to the kite of the labour unions, we are playing second fiddle to John Mitchell in the legislation which we are adopting in this House. We are dealing with this labour question in the interest of the unions ; we do not take into consideration the interests of the great mass of labourers who do not desire to join the unions, the men who want to sell their labour, who want to be at liberty to make a bargain for their labour without being told by officers of the labour union whether they shall have the privileges of a citizen in making such a contract or not. The weapon of the greater portion

of the strikes in the United States has been the terrorism that has been exercised by the trade unions in preventing men from working who desired to work, who were satisfied to work, who were satisfied with the wages that they were receiving, and who desired to go on earning those wages. But they have been prevented from doing so, have been compelled to cease labour at the dictation of a tyrannical organization, an organization which, if it has the power, will exercise a tyranny greater than has ever been exercised in this country.
Is the hon. gentleman opposed to trades unions ?

I am not opposed to trades unions when they are operated within legitimate and proper limits, but I am opposed to trades unions that usurp to themselves authority to command the entire labour interests of the country, and to coerce and compel men in every direction to join the unions whether they wish to do so or not, and who, if they do not -wish to join the unions, will resort to violence, to murder and to arson, in order to carry out their purposes. Now, Sir, I propose to offer an amendment to this subsection 6, or subsection 8, as it will be. The section reads now as follows
In no case shall a conciliator or arbitrator stipulate, nor shall it be stipulated in any agreement promoted or recommended by a con-cilator or arbitrator, that any employee shall relinquish his membership in any local, national or international trades union or labour association ; nor shall an agreement subject any employee to a penalty on account of such membership.
I propose to add these words :
Or discriminate against persons who are not members of trades unions or labour associations.

I venture to think that if the Minister of Labour had drawn a clause it would not be worded as this clause 6a. I would have thought it was unnecessary for any member of this House to express himself with regard to trades unions in discussing a measure such as this, which is a simple piece of legislation. But as others have so expressed themselves, in order that by my silence I may not be misunderstood, I desire to say that I sympathize as much as any member in this House with the desire of the labouring classes to promote their interests by forming themselves into labour associations. The question before this House is whether this particular clause, 6a, is, under the circumstances, a reasonable and proper clause, and if adopted by this House, will it be a reasonable piece of legislation. Now, when we consider that the Act which is being amended is not an arbitration Act at all, but a conciliation Act, when we find that the conciliator has no power to bind either the employer or the employee, I venture to say that this is, I was going to say, a monstrous thing.
103i
In what way ?

The arbitrator has no power to bind the party. You may call him the conciliator or an arbitrator, but it comes down to the same result, that he has no power to bind the parties. Now, if an arbitrator had power to bind the employer or the employee, and if there were machinery to enforce his decision, then I could understand the propriety of such a clause as this. But when the conciliator or arbitrator has no power to bind the parties, I venture to say that it is a most extraordinary piece of legislation to forbid him even to make a suggestion.
Supposing both parties agreed to abide by his proposition ?

If they left the matter to the arbitrator to decide for them, he could not put this particular clause in, even if it were a proper clause. I am not saying that the case might not arise when it would be proper for the conciliator to insert any such clause as this, but it is conceivable.

Supposing in the longshoremen's strike in Montreal an agreement was entered into by a third party that the workmen should drop their membership in a labour organization, would that agreement be affected by this clause ?

Practically it would make a difference, for this reason, if this clause were passed the conciliator or arbitrator would not be allowed to put in such a clause as is forbidden here, but if this clause does not pass, and if the conciliator or arbitrator did insert such a clause without having any machinery to enforce it, nobody would be bound by it. I would like to ask my hon. friend in turn if this is a reasonable clause, and I want to go further ; if it is proper to say that no conciliator or arbitrator shall say that no employee shall relinquish his membership in any association. I would go further and say that no employer should relinquish his membership in any association. If it is fair for one side, why not make it reciprocal, and apply it to the other side as well ?
I do not suppose they would have any objection to that.

I do not say that they would. But I think that if it is a good thing for one it should be good for all. I am not advocating that principle; I am rather advocating another principle because it seems to me we are doing a wholly unnecessary act in putting a clause on the statute-book which will not result in any good. The clause seems to assume that under no possible circumstances, no matter what the provocation might be, could the friends of the union go so far astray that a conciliator might be justified in saying that a man should leave the union. I do not know that

they will go so far astray that an honest impartial conciliator would adopt this principle, but if they have gone so far astray it seems to me rather hard that in any conciliation effort he should he deprived of making that suggestion. Therefore, I think this should be reciprocal; if it is applied to one it should be applied to the other, and secondly, because it would be faulty legislation I would be inclined to oppose the clause.

Every one who knows anything about labour disputes knows perfectly well that there is no instance he could name where any labour organizations have taken objection to a manufacturer simply because he belongs to the Manufacturers' Association. We all know that perfectly well, and we who have watched these disputes also know that there never has been a labour dispute between organized labour and organized capital in which the question of membership in the labour organization was not the real point of the contention as between the two parties. It is true that the wage difficulty arises very frequently, but oftener the difficulty is by reason of men belonging to labour organizations. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) finds fault with these tyrannical organizations which commit murder and violence. There is not a man who belongs to a labour organization in Canada that I know of who wants to commit murder or exercise tyranny or anything of that kind. These men simply want to associate themselves together for mutual benefit and protection. I hold that any man who asks that privilege is entitled to it.

My remark in regard to violence and intimidation on the part of members connected with labour organizations referred to the operations of labour unions in the United States, and not to Canadian organizations at all, and it was made in connection with this matter of international unions.
Then what was the object in bringing that question into this discussion ?
I referred to international affiliations.

We know perfectly well that in Chicago and other cities in the United States they have gone altogether too far. They have committed tyranny, and they have committed murder in many cases. I do not know a single instance in Canada where they uphold conduct of that kind. I am quite sure they do not.
Mr.. BROCK. Why was it necessary for the authorities in Montreal to call out the troops ?
The troops were called out because we had not sufficient police in Montreal.
What for ?
There was no conflict; they were literally called out in place of the police.
Called out because a conflict was threatened.
During all the discussion that took place in this House about longshoremen's strike not a single instance of violence was brought to the notice of the House.

Why, was not the calling out of the troops a most extraordinary evidence of fear on the part of the authorities in Montreal that violence was going to be committed ? Otherwise they were absolutely wrong in calling out the troops.

I might refer to an instance in the hon. gentleman's own city of Toronto. No one will charge the students of the different colleges with being tyrannical or wishing to commit murder or violence ; yet the troops were called out to take charge of these young men.
Certainly.

I take it that the circumstances in Montreal and in Toronto were on the same lines. It was not so much the fault of the students as a certain class of people who take advantage of a procession of that kind in order to create violence.
Show me your company and I will tell you what you are.

If I were to judge all the students by that I am afraid I would have to say that they were in bad company that night. I think if the disturbers who usually accompany these processions had not been there, there would not have been so much done about that Toronto affair as really was done. In respect to this measure I do not see why a man has not the right to belong to a labour organization if he sees fit. Most of these disputes hinge largely on the question of men belonging to a labour organization or retaining membership in an organization. I cannot see why they should be deprived of that privilege. I am not one of those who uphold labour organizations in depriving other men of the privileges of obtaining employment because they are not members of the organization. Possibly some go a little farther than they should. I think that they have a right to be organized and that they are entitled to exercise all the privileges of their organizations. They are entitled to the right to organize just as much as manufacturers are, as legal gentlemen are, as medical gentlemen are, or as any other bodies of men are.

I think it is to be regretted that in the discussion of this Bill hon. gentlemen should have thought it necessary to

refer to some of the things that they have referred to; for instance, to injurious labour organizations, red-headed agitators and so on-bogies which have been deliberately planted in the public mind. I think it would have been a great deal better to have discussed this Bill which is intended to be a conciliation Bill. The question that was brought up by the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) is a very material point in reference in this subject, it is that after all the one thing that is the pith and heart of the labour dispute is the question that is called recognition. Half the troubles that are on to-day might be settled tomorrow if it were not for the question of recognition. I have often said that I believed in compulsory arbitration. Compulsory arbitration recognizes that a dispute must be between two parties and not between an organization of capital and any individual employees. It will only deal with organizations on both sides. Then, it is possible for you to get men into a frame of mind to see that there are two strong sides which are brought together by the conciliation process. Compulsory arbitration brings labour disputes up to date. It is no good discussing the labour question as if labour organizations will be put to one side. They will not be put to one side. They are growing stronger just as organizations of capital are growing stronger, and any movement that is going to affect arbitration or conciliation has got to recognize that fact. After all, this clause it not so hurriedly or awkwardly drawn as some suppose. It is not a clause that has been got together especially for this Act. It is one that is beginning to appear in the Conciliation Acts of different countries. There is a good principle in it, and I will explain why. When an award is made to settle a dispute, there is this one thing that makes that award of no effect whatever, and that is anything that prevents the affiliation of employees with the union that has been in the dispute. Why, because if they have not got that organization at their back under which they struck, their settlement is no good. The employer accepts the settlement and immediately disregards it, because there is no other side to enforce the settlement. I say that in any proposition that is made by disinterested parties it is wise that they should leave this question where they found it; leave it to be settled between the men themselves, but do not take the dispute away from the organization, and do not fine any man for his affiliation with a union. If you do that, you will immediately destroy all confidence in conciliation. There is not much confidence in conciliation in this country at the present time, and it is because of the actual experience that this has been attempted and some times has been successfully done in perfectly well meant conciliations. In bringing in a disinterested party, you bring in a person who does not understand the organization of labour or the organization of capital, and it appears quite reasonable to such a one that these parties should work together as individuals, as he has the notion they used to do in the past. It is no use attempting to conciliate on the basis of individuals working with an employer-the whole thing now is two strong parties, necessarily antagonists for the time being, perhaps antagonistic all through ; the interest of the country is to bring them together. That is the idea of this Conciliation Act. It seems to me regrettable that in discussing this matter we should in any way appeal to passion or to ideas that are at all events out of date.

As the Minister of Labour has taken this Bill under his fatherly consideration, we have the right to ask him what is his opinion of the amendment suggested by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) ? The minister's opinion would no doubt have a beneficial, effect in enabling us to reach a wise decision as to whether we should adopt this amendment or not. I am glad we have cleared the atmosphere a good deal by the discussion that has taken place this evening. My hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) has put himself right. The attempt had been made to show that he is opposed to the organization of Canadian workmen into unions. He has told us that he is not opposed to that. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) was charged here with saying that he had referred to labour unions in this country as containing men who would commit murder.
I do not wish to be misrepresented

I am trying to put the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) right as well as my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock). I say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) was charged here with saying that Canadian unions contained men, some of whom were prepared to commit murder. The hon. gentleman has repudiated that, and he says he refers to American unions. The only difference of opinion between the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) and some other gentlemen who are in favour of labour organizations is as to what is meant by an international union. The Canadian labour unions are affiliated with these international bodies, because in union there is strength. The Canadian unions do not affiliate for any improper purpose. They are bound to support each other, but they are not united to injure any one. That is the principle on which they amalgamate. They do not lose any of their rights by amalgamating with labour organizations on the other side of the line; they rather strengthen the union organization. I am not satisfied yet, Mr. Chairman, that it has been proven that any person has come from the American side for the purpose of organizing our men into unions so as to

compel them to strike to the detriment of their own interests. I am open to argument, and I invite and challenge any hon. member on either side of this committee to-night to make good the allegation that men have come here to organize Canadians into unions and to compel them to strike. X say that statement cannot be made good, and It is not fair that such a statement should be made and that hon. members who do not know anything about union men, should be misled and deceived by such a statement. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) strikes out the words ' local, national or international,' I cannot see what objection can be raised to that amendment. It seems to cover the whole case. We are only legislating here, after all, for our own unions; we cannot legislate for unions on the other side, except to punish them if they come over here to commit a crime.

In answer to my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), I do not think it should be the part of any board of conciliators or arbitrators to interfere with the freedom of any citizen to do whatever it is lawful for him to do, whether he choses to belong to a union or not to belong to a union.
Hear, hear.

I think that to do otherwise would be an act of tyranny. You might as well stipulate that a man must not belong to a particular church or to a particular political party. I think that it would be entirely improper for us to interfere with the freedom of our citizens, and therefore I quite approve of a man's rights being preserved, and if necessary that we should do so by legislation. I may say that but for this Bill I would not have thought that any conciliator would have attempted in a proposed basis of settlement, to deprive a party to a labour dispute of his right either to belong or not to belong to a union as he sees fit. In taking that general view, I believe that it is just as proper that we should protect * nonunion ' as ' union ' labour.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

Therefore, I would have no objection to the amendment of my hon. friend from North Norfolk, which is that we should not discriminate against non-union labour. The same principle would apply, I suppose.
Would it not be well for the minister to prepare an amendment that would meet that case ?
The hon. member (Mr. Clarke) has suggested to strike out these qualifying words.
I agree to accept the amendment of the hon. member for North Norfolk. His amendment is a great deal more reasonable than his speech.
Hear, hear.
I would like to persuade him (Mr. Charlton) if I can, that there are two reasonable men in the House, if he considers he is one. I move to strike out the words : ' Local, international, or national.'

The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) spoke to us of not objecting to foreign capital coming into our country. I think foreign capital means foreign cash. What does international labour mean ? It can do a certain amount of harm, but is it anything that can be attacked ? Foreign capital coming to this country is under Canadian laws, and If it does damage to any individual in this country there is a means of getting justice, and collecting damages. But organized labour such as has been threatened here; what does it bring ? It brings with it of necessity the calling out of the troops of this country to protect, not foreign capital, but Canadian capital from damage and from loss. We have seen in the last few days in the public press where 4,000 labourers-I do not say they are members of labour unions, but it shows you the company that labour unions bring in its train in this country; it shows that all the scruff of this country come out to assist them and to protect them to derail cars, to destroy property, to stone people, who are engaged in their lawful calling. I do not mean to say that this is done by organized labour, but this is the affiliation; this is the company they keep; this is the kind of sympathy they bring out; not the sympathy of people whose opinions are worth having, but the very worst elements of the whole country are brought out to sympathize with and to back up these strikes brought about by organized labour.
Then they defy us to bring forward evidences of these men being invited to come to this country. If this House will give me a committee, I shall have no difficulty in proving not only that they have come here, but that they have been asked to come here. Nobody, under these circumstances, can invest capital in this country with any degree of safety, because they know that they are liable to be held up by what is called organized labour. The labour organizations of this country are not in favour of strikes. Give them, a chance to vote by ballot, and they will not vote for strikes. But men do not want to be called scabs on the streets ; they do not want their children coming from school to be hooted at; they do not want their wives to be insulted on the streets. But ten men in a hundred can bring about a strike, and there is no means of getting at them. These people can shoot from behind a hedge, and then run away, and there is no way of reaching them. This is a kind of thing which men who have respect for themselves despise. If the matter were left to a vote by ballot, I know the way that vote would go. I have been in

Toronto in the last few days, and I know the feeling among the labour men there, and they are not in favour of strikes. Only 10 per cent of the workers in Toronto are labour union men. I do not see why this country should be terrorized by them. I am prepared to meet the labouring people anywhere, and to convince any honest, reasonable man that there are two sides to this question. Labour has no right to terrorize over capital. I am prepared to protect organized labour, organized under Canadian law, and responsible for any harm it does to capital, and I am prepared to make capital responsible for any harm it does to labour.
I wish to place myself right on this matter. My battle is with international organizations. If we stamp them out in this country we can deal with our own people, who, I believe, are quite reasonable. I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). You need only pick up the papers to see how true his statement is, that these people do not stop even at murder. No less than twelve people were murdered yesterday, not by organized labour, but by the scruff of the country which they have in their train.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to say a word on this question ; but after having listened to the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), I think it is due to myself and due to those whom I represent to say that my views on this labour problem are diametrically the opposite of his. That hon. gentleman has referred to those men who have organized as a labour party as men who will shoot at you from behind a hedge. I deny it ; it is not true ; and if the hon. member can give an instance of that, it is probable we may be in a position
The hon. gentleman must be intentionally obtuse

I suggested the possibility of a labour party being such as would do that kind of thing. I did not accuse any labour man of doing it.
Then 1 say that unless the hon. member for Centre Toronto produces some facts upon which this House can form an opinion, he has no right to make that wholesale statement.
I have made it, and I stick to it.

I know the hon. member has made it, and that is the objection I take to it-that statements of that kind are made absolutely without foundation. Now, we know that the hon. member is the head of many industrial concerns in this country, including several large manufacturing concerns. He has had strikes ; he has had labour difficulties ; but will the hon. member rise in his place and say that as a result
of a single strike or a single labour difficulty which he has experienced, there has been one single act of violence or one single act of unjust treatment ? I say he cannot. The hon. gentleman contends that men have no right to organize under an international union. I submit that they have that right. They have a right to organize just as they see fit, whether the union be national or international. The difficulty in organizing a national union to-day is that workmen can be imported from the United States to take the place of men who think they have been wronged and have gone on strike ; and the force of an international union is that men cannot be imported in that way, because they will not come when they are invited. I say that so far the unions in Canada have acted within the law, and have acted in a most reasonable way. Never yet, so far as I know, has there been an unreasonable or criminal act committed by a single union man who has been on strike. I believe that the principle of this Bill should be adopted by this House. Conciliation is what we all aim at. Conciliation is the means that will bring about the best results both to labour and capital ; and speeches like that delivered to-night by the hon. member for Centre Toronto only serve to augment any difficulty which may exist between labour and capital. I believe Sir, that the course adopted by the Minister of Labour is the best means for bringing labour and capital together in Canada ; and if the hon. minister will continue to pursue the course he has undertaken, he will do more to bring about a better understanding between labour and capital than any arbitrary measure that this House can adopt, while the speech of the hon. member for Centre Toronto only augments the furore.
Before the hon. gentleman sits down, will he kindly name any strike that has occurred in any company with which I have been connected ?
Yes, I will mention the strike which occurred two weeks ago in the Hespeler Woollen Mills, of which the hon. gentleman is president, and which employees 500 hands.
How long did it last ?
I do not know.
You should know. It was settled inside of twelve hours. They did not lose a day's pay. There was no international union connected with it. We dealt with the men directly.

They may not have lost a day's pay, and I congratulate the hon. gentleman on that fact. If the demands of men were considered in that spirit, and their reasonable demands granted, there would be far fewer strikes. I say the principle of the Bill is right, and it ought to be adopted. The principle of this Bill was adopted when

this government came into power, and when the Minister of Labour took control of labour troubles in this country. While the name of Sir William Mu-lock may go down to posterity, it will not only go down as the Postmaster General, but it will also go down as Minister of Labour.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 4, as amended by striking out the words ' local, national or international,' be adopted?

I wish to call the attention of the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) to the fact that if this amendment should carry, it implies the recognition of not only local, national or international unions, but of unions which may not even be international. The amendment includes not only local, national and international, but even foreign labour organizations. I am in favour of the amendment, but it does not meet the point raised by the hon. member for Centre Toronto. I do not believe myself that a man should be required to relinquish his membership in any organization. We have discussed this matter tonight widely and brought a good deal into the discussion not to be found within the confines of the Bill, but, as my hon. friend from West Toronto lias said, it is as well probably to clear the air. In my opinion it would be better if the labour organizations of this country were purely Canadian. I think that we should endeavour to make everything in this country more Canadian ; and when we have foreign presidents and officers of our labour organizations, we are not encouraging that sentiment. But while it would no doubt be better to have Canadian officers for Canadian unions, the very worst way to endeavour to bring that about would be to try to coerce the labouring men into adopting that opinion. The very worst way to bring about a sentiment of that kind is to talk of labour organizations as cowardly organizations and unmanly. So long as we find hon. members holding out the red rag to the bull, so to speak, we are not going to reach the end desired of making these organizations thoroughly Canadian, officered by Canadian men. The other evening, in speaking on this Bill, I said that I thought it would be well to have an inquiry into the labour question of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. While the questions of the tariff, public works and railway transportation are great questions, that which is going to be the most important within the next ten years is the question of labour and capital. Every morning we read in the press of new labour difficulties, of new strikes, declared in various parts of Canada, and if the wave of prosperity should recede at any time, these labour troubles will be accentuated. No doubt the question often occurs to the capitalist, not in this country alone, but in every country to-day. whether he should invest his money in manufacturing enterprises for fear that the

demands of labour will destroy the fruits of his industry, and we should seriously consider whether there is not some way of arranging matters between labour and capital on a more satisfactory basis. Sly hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), in referring to labour organizations, said that he was willing that men should vote by ballot. Well, there is not a labouring organization in Canada in which the vote is not taken by ballot when a strike is proposed, and before foreigners are called in. We have no right to refer to the leaders of our labouring men as agitators. If our men in Canada are willing to serve under the leadership of Americans in their councils and unions, it is not in good taste to refer to these leaders whom they have chosen as agitators. Let me repeat that, even with a foreign president and officers at the head of these labour organizations, no strike can be declared in the Dominion without a secret ballot first being taken. Not until the men have declared by secret ballot in favour of a strike can a strike be declared, or any of the foreign officers of the union be called in. While it would be more Canadian and national if our labour unions were officered by Canadians, still you cannot coerce the labouring men. Let us therefore endeavour, on more amiable and conciliatory lines, to cultivate among our labouring people the opinion that it will be more in their interest in every way to have their organizations and unions officered by men of their own nationality.
In discussing this clause I will endeavour to confine my remarks to the clause itself. I would ask if it is in order to discuss on this clause the various phases of the labour question ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The discussion has been quite irregular, and I would ask hon. members of the committee to come back to the provision before us.

It seems to me that the discussion has not only gone beyond the provisions of this Bill, but that we have been taking up the time of this House in considering legislation which we will have no power to make any practical use of. After we have adopted this measure, we will have no means of compelling either one side or the other to be governed by it or to accept any awai'd which it may enable us to make. It seems to me that the only object of this Bill-the only effect it has had or can possibly have-is to enable those who represent the labour unions and professional sympathizers with labour to spread themselves and speak to the gallery. It has certainly been taken advantage of to-night for this puipose, and in this connection to attribute opinions to the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), to which I am sure the majority of this House will agree with me in saying, he never gave

expression when speaking on this Bill. The hon. gentleman who last addressed the House spoke about flaunting the red rag to the bull and agitators, and all that kind of thing. I do not know what sort of a constituency the hon. gentleman represents, but I do not believe that my hon. friend for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) would make use of any expressions calculated to create the impression that he is opposed to the labour of this country. Why, everybody knows that he employs a great many men, everybody knows that he furnishes work and money for many more men-in all probability for one thousand men to every one employed by the hon. gentleman who has taken this opportunity to indulge in this very paltry attack. How many of these men, I may ask, employ labourers ? How many of the lawyers who have found it necessary to spread themselves and wave their arms here tonight are employing one hundred, or twenty-five, or ten men-or even one, unless it be an underpaid clerk ? Mr. Chairman, the fact is this, that without capital, labour is of very little use ; and it iis when labour is at its highest and when men are drawing probably the highest wages they have drawn for ten years, at a time when they can afford to waste time, that they turn a willing ear to the agitator, and the agitator is always there ready to take advantage of the opportunity. And I have no hesitation in saying-and I have watched this question with considerable interest-that just such Acts as we have listened to to-night are what very frequently leave the labourer without his hire. For the capitalist is not obliged to put his money out in precarious undertakings; and when the labourer becomes so exacting as he is becoming in Canada today and throughout the United States, capital draws in and says, Well, we don't have to continue those worring misunderstandings. We can get along very satisfactorily by keeping our money in the savings banks, and we know which side suffers then. But we have so many men in Canada and in the United States who are so anxious to stand well with this labouring element that as I have said before, in order to win this vote, they are ready to assent to things that do harm both to labour and to capital, but the greatest harm to the men they pretend to serve.
Amendment (Mr. Puttee) adopted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment moved by Mr. Charlton be adopted ?
What is the meaning of that amendment ?
That persons not members of labour associations or trades unions shall not be discriminated against in the settlement of labour disputes.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) think that this accomplishes the object lie has in view ?

I think so.
Amendment (Mr. Charlton) adopted.
Bill, as amended, reported.
House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Charlton : that Bill (No. 106) to amend the Act to restrict the importation and employment of aliens, be now read a second time.
I desire to make a very few remarks upon this Bill
I think the hon. member (Mr. Charlton) has already spoken.
I move the adjournment of the debate.
I think the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Ross) who moves the motion to adjourn the debate, seconded the motion for the second reading of the Bill.
If permitted to speak on the motion to adjourn the debate-
I do not think I am able to put the motion to adjourn the debate, because the hon. member who moved it himself seconded the motion for the second reading of the Bill.
The non. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) this afternoon had extended to him the courtesy of three or four minutes-
There is no motion before the Chair, except the second reading of the Bill.
I move the adjournment of the debate.

I presume the motion will carry. I am under great obligation co my hon. friend who has kindly come to my rescue, and I think his motion will stand as a motion and probably be acted upon by the House in the affirmative. However. I desire to say a few words with reference to the Bill that is now under consideration of this House. The Alien Labour Law of 1897, in section five, chapter eleven, provided that new industries established for the first time in Canada might employ skilled labour brought from abroad in cases where such labour was unobtainable in Canada. This provision did not apply to industries already in existence. The Bill I have the honour to offer to the House proposes to expunge the words ' in or upon any new industries not at present established in Canada,' and to provide that skilled labour may be employed upon industries in Canada

provided such skilled labour is not obtainable in this country. Now, I am unable to understand why any discrimination should under the provisions of this Act of 1897, have been made against the established industries of this country, why, this provision should have been made to apply only to new industries being established here for the first time. I venture to think that in no other country in the world has such a provision been adopted or is such a provision in force.
The Alien Labour Law, of which this provision is a part, was, in my opinion, founded altogether upon false principles. It was adopted-perhaps I am not entitled to say avowedly-but it was adopted as we all know in retaliation for a similar law of the United States, a most unjust and abused law, passed by congress and enforced in that country. Now, this American law, absurd in its operations, was one that we copied in the provision made in this chapter eleven of the statutes of 1897, and it is a Jaw that has not been enforced in the United States against Canada, it is so manifestly abused that public opinion there does not require its enforcement. To-day hundreds of persons cross from Windsor to Detroit every morning and engage in operations in that city, every one of whom could be turned back if the Alien Law were enforced. The same is being done at Buffalo and a number of other towns on the frontier. Labour from the Canadian side passes over unimpeded and in violation of the provisions of the Alien Labour Law; yet we have a law on the statute-book here which, in so far as these provisions about skilled labour is concerned is, if not rigidly enforced, is so much of an impediment to the manufacturers as to be found by them very oppressive in its operation, and very detrimental to their interests.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman name one manufacturer who has suffered on account of this law.

Yes, I will name myself; and I can procure for the hon. gentleman many names of manufacturers. This Bill was put into my hands by the Manufacturers' Association with a representation that the operaton of this Bill was very detrimental to their interests. Now, in this age, there is a keen competition between manufacturing nations. The manufacturing interests of Great Britain, the manufacturing interests of Germany, add of Russia, and of the United States for that matter, are keenly alive to the importance of adopting new and improved machinery ; and in all these nations anything that is invented that lessens the cost of production is at once seized upon by active and progressive manufacturers. The invention of new machinery has in the United States given that country the lead in the boot and shoe trade, in
various other lines of business. The boot and shoe trade machinery in the United (States, machinery for the production of pig iron, for the manipulation of steel, and various other lines of manufacture, are imported into Germany, into Great Britain, into Russia, and with this machinery it becomes necessary in most cases to send skilled labour from the country where the machinery is invented to the country where it is to be put into operation. Now, under this law a Canadian manufacturer is unable to avail himself of the advantages that will be conferred upon the country by the introduction of new and improved machinery that is calculated to reduce the cost of production in his particular line of business, because he is prohibited by law from importing the labour that is necessary to put that machinery into operation, to run it and to teach Canadian operators how to run it.
The labour unions, I suppose, are unfavourable to this provision. I think they stand in their own light in this matter, and fail to understand the scope of the operation of this measure. If there was no impediment in the way of introducing new machinery to give the manufacturers the facilities that they think necessary to put that improved machinery into operation. The law is utterly absurd. The law does not propose to give to the manufacturers the right to employ skilled labour or to bring in skilled labour that is obtainable in Canada. The Bill simply provides that those provisions regarding skilled labour should be applied to all manufacturing interests; that the skilled labour can be imported for carrying on these manufacturing operations if that skilled labour is not obtainable in this country. Well, who can object to that ? What possible objection can there be to the permission given to manufacturers to improve their methods of production and bring in the most modern and up-to-date machinery to enable them to compete with their rivals in the United States and other countries ? They have got to do it if they are going to hold their place in the race. But this law which prohibit them from obtaining artisans and experts that can put that machinery up, and run it, and teach others to run it, is a law detrimental to the manufacturing industries of Canada. Certainly we ought to afford to the manufacturing interests reasonable protection, reasonable advantages, reasonable privileges. We ought not to debar them from the introduction of methods. and means, and machinery that will permit them to reduce the cost of production, to increase the effectiveness of their staff, and to bring them into competition with other manufacturing interests that have all these appliances. The provision that prohibits the employment or the introduction of skilled labour if it is obtainable in Canada will protect the interest of skilled labour here, and will prevent any abuse. The manufacturer is not going to import skilled

labour at a bigh cost or bring it from abroad if he can get it in Canada, and if he can get it fifty or sixty per cent cheaper. In no case will the manufacturer import skilled labour that is obtainable in this country, and in that fact is a safeguard against abuse in reference to this matter. I therefore beg to move the second reading of this Bill, which eliminates the provision with regard to established industries and permits any manufacturing industry in Canada to import skilled labour where that labour is not obtainable in this country.

My hon. friend suggests that the necessity for this amendment arises from the fact that occasionally there is a change of machinery in old established industries, and that there is no labour in Canada capable of working the new machinery. Perhaps such a state of affairs from time to time does exist. But I would rather think that in the introduction of new machinery to-day there is quite enough ingenuity amongst the workmen engaged in our industries to enable them in a short time, and with proper educational advantages afforded them, to learn how to make use of this new machinery. I recollect one instance in point. I remember quite well what was supposed to be an intricate new piece of machinery, having been introduced by an established industry, and there were no skilled labourers in Canada capable of working that machinery. The employer came to me and asked me what he ought to do. It was not for me to guide him but I intimated to him a very simple method by which he might get over the difficulty. Instead of importing an army of skilled workmen to work the machines I suggested that he might get some one to teach the men in his employ to use these machines. He did so and in a short time he had these men, Canadians, working these machines. Such a course as this might get over many of the difficulties to which my hon. friend alludes. To make the amendment we perhaps would open the door to an abuse of the Act, which my hon. friend knows was placed on the statute-book not from choice but from necessity. Therefore, I would favour the amendment of the hon. member for Cumberland Mr. Logan) that the debate stand adjourned.
Amendment (Mr. Logan) agreed to, and debate adjourned.

speechtext: Mr. BICKERDIKE moved the second reading of Bill (No. 133) to prohibit the importation, manufacture, or sale of cigarettes.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF THE IMPORTATION, MANUFACTURE, OR SALE OF CIGARETTES.
speechtext:
I have to declare in regard to this Bill that I do not consider it has been properly introduced, and for the following reasons : When this Bill was introduced the other day, I did not then have the opportunity of reading it over before its introduction, and I was then unable to declare whether it should have originated in committee of the whole House, or whether it should have been introduced on a motion for leave. I see now that the Bill has for its object to prohibit the manufacture and sale of any cigarette or cigarette papers, and the Bill also provides that no cigarette or cigarette papers shall be imported into the country. It was suggested the other day, when the Bill was introduced, that such a measure could only be brought in by a member of the administration, and not by a private member, because it affects the revenue. The contention concerned was an erroneous construction of our parliamentary law, because according to our rule 86, which governs the point raised the other day, it is provided that the House cannot provide any vote for the apportioning of any part of the public revenue, and cannot impose any tax or impost that has not been first recommended to the House by the Governor. This Bill, though dealing with the question of tariff, does not impose any tax or impost, and it can then be introduced by a private member. But when introduced by a private member, the proposition should

be first considered in a committee of the whole House. A Bill relating to trade and to alteration of the laws concerning trade should originate in committee of the whole House. By section 41, of our rules, it is provided as follows :
No Bill relating to trade, or alteration of the laws concerning trade is to be brought Into the House until the proposition shall have been first considered in the Committee of the Whole House, and agreed unto by the House.
This enactment has generally been followed in the Commons of Great Britain, as in the legislative assembly of the colonies having constitutional government, though they have not in England, as in some of the colonies, a rule as formally expressed as it is in our procedure, as you may see by Bourinot, pages 591 and 592. We have in England as well as in this country certain precedents on the matter. I will not undertake to quote them all, but I would be permitted to refer to a precedent of 1883, which is to be found in the ' Commons Journal,' page 377, where a Bill to regulate the sale of or prohibit the traffic in intoxicating liquors originated in committee. In 1885 a Bill to amend certain portions of the License Act, of 1883 was initiated in committee. In 1S80 and 1885, a Bill regulating the sale of fertilizers originated also in committee, and in 1886, a Bill regulating the manufacture and sale of oleo-margarine and butterine also originated in committee. I then come to the conclusion that this Bill was not properly introduced in the House, and the fact of presenting it on motion for leave would be a departure from the usage which has been adhered to in numerous instances and precedents. I declare the motion for its second reading as being irregular and out of order.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF THE IMPORTATION, MANUFACTURE, OR SALE OF CIGARETTES.
speechtext:
Whilst I shall bow respectfully to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, I would draw your attention to the fact that I was going to move that the House resolve itself into Committee of the Whole. I would refer you to the decision of Mr. Speaker Cockburn, given in 1868, which is as follows:
The procedure on a Bill which ought to have originated in Committee of the Whole, but which has been read a first time by leave of the House, can be proceeded with when the House has subsequently resolved itself into Committee of the Whole, and adopted the resolution on which the Bill is based.

speechtext: That has not been followed in this case. In the case quoted by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) the resolution had been adopted in Committee of the Whole when the second reading of the Bill came up for discussion. In this instance the same procedure has not been followed.
